newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Kuehbacher casts new doubt on EMU date.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Kuehbacher casts new doubt on EMU date.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, in unusually strong words for a member of the German central bank, said on Tuesday that delay of European economic and monetary union (EMU) was the only option if Germany does not strictly fulfil the Maastricht Treaty.

In an interview with "Boerse Online" magazine, Kuehbacher said he saw little chance that Bonn would be able to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product as is mandated for nations hoping to join monetary union and that failure to do so meant delaying EMU.

"If I interpret the criteria verbatim, as Finance Minister Theo Waigel has always demanded, and if I look at the ruling of the Constitutional Court, delay is the only consequence, unless the Federal government still manages to limit the deficit to three percent of GDP."
Kuehbacher, who has raised the possibility of an EMU delay before, said, however, that it appeared unlikely that Germany would meet Maastricht Treaty targets.
"In view of the current economic developments I have my doubts," Kuehbacher said of a punctual 1999 EMU start.
Kuehbacher's comments are the latest sign that Germany may be tilting towards deciding on a delay in monetary union, despite reassurances from Bonn that Maastricht targets will be met.
The magazine said the interview was conducted last Wednesday and will go on news stands tomorrow.
Kuehbacher said that Germany was in an especially difficult position in its fight to trim its budget deficit which in 1996 stood at 3.8 percent of gross domestic product.
Raising taxes, he said, would hamper Germany's tenuous economic recovery.

With many private research institutes predicting a deficit between 3.25 percent to 3.5 percent, the government would need to find a way to either increase revenues or cut spending by around 15 billion marks ($8.9 billion) in order to qualify for EMU, he said.
Kuehbacher said the debate about delay will come to a head in May when tax estimates are due and the government receives what will likely be news of disappointing revenues.
"The government will no longer be able to shirk the decision on whether to delay EMU," he said, calling on Bonn to make a decision on EMU delay as quickly as possible.
As have others on the Bundesbank council, Kuehbacher sounded warnings about starting EMU if the Maastricht criteria were not fully met.

"The worst case from my point of view would be if we go ahead with the decision with a missed criterion," he said. "If Germany heads for 1999 as the starting date regardless of the consequences, the government risks enormous turbulence in financial markets."
Kuebacher's comments come on the back of remarks made by Finance Minister Waigel on Tuesday that fuelled worries in financial markets that EMU will be delayed.
Speaking in Brussels, Waigel stressed that adherence to the Maastricht Treaty's convergence criteria took precedence over the timetable for monetary union.
The remark sparked one of the steepest falls in the German Bund futures in months, weakness which continued today after Kuebacher spoke of delay. ($ = 1.690 German Marks)
